title: Intune proactive remediations
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Build self-healing endpoints with Intune proactive remediations: a detection script that finds a problem and a remediation script that fixes it, deployed and reported at fleet scale.
objectives: Explain the detection-plus-remediation script pair model and its exit-code contract
Write a detection script that exits 1 only when remediation is needed
Write a matching remediation script that fixes the issue idempotently
Understand the SYSTEM vs user context and 64-bit execution settings
Interpret detection and remediation status output in the Intune reports
Deploy a remediation to a device group and read pre/post remediation results

quiz.q: In a proactive remediation, what does an exit code of 1 from the detection script mean?
options: An issue was detected, so the remediation script should run
quiz.why: By contract, detection exit 0 means compliant (no action), and exit 1 means an issue was detected and triggers the remediation script on that device.

quiz.q: Why must a remediation script be idempotent?
options: So running it repeatedly on already-fixed devices causes no harm and produces the same end state
Because Intune only runs it once ever
So it can run without PowerShell
quiz.why: Remediations run on a schedule, so re-running on an already-healthy device must be safe and produce the same correct state without side effects or errors.

quiz.q: By default, in which security context does a proactive remediation run?
options: The local SYSTEM account, unless you choose to run it in the user context
A domain admin account you supply
quiz.why: Remediations run as SYSTEM by default; you can opt to run them in the logged-on user's context, which matters for HKCU registry keys and per-user settings.

quiz.q: What should detection write to standard output to make Intune reporting useful?
options: A short single-line status string via Write-Output describing the finding
quiz.why: The last line written to stdout is surfaced as the pre/post-remediation output in Intune reports, so a concise status string makes triage and reporting far easier.

quiz.q: Name the setting you must enable when a remediation needs to read 64-bit registry or program paths.
quiz.answer: Run script in 64-bit PowerShell (set to Yes); otherwise the script runs in 32-bit and may be redirected to WOW6432Node or miss 64-bit paths.
quiz.why: By default scripts can run 32-bit; enabling 64-bit execution prevents registry/file-system redirection from hiding the real 64-bit state on modern Windows.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why split logic into separate detection and remediation scripts rather than one script that fixes everything?
quiz.answer: Detection-only runs let you measure how widespread an issue is and report on it without changing devices, and only the affected machines incur the remediation, which is safer and observable.
quiz.why: The pair model gives you a reporting/measurement phase and a controlled fix phase, so you can pilot, quantify impact, and avoid touching healthy devices.

body_markdown:
## Self-healing endpoints, by design

A **proactive remediation** (now called a **remediation** in Intune) is a pair of PowerShell scripts that run on a schedule via the **Intune Management Extension**: a **detection** script that decides whether a problem exists, and a **remediation** script that fixes it. The two scripts communicate through a strict **exit-code contract**.

- Detection **exit 0** = healthy, do nothing.
- Detection **exit 1** = problem found, run the remediation.

This pair model lets you first *measure* how widespread an issue is across the fleet before you ever change a device.

## Writing the detection script

Detection should be fast, read-only, and decisive. Output a short status string (it appears in the Intune report), then exit with the right code.

```powershell
# Detect: is the Windows Time service running and automatic?
$svc = Get-Service -Name 'W32Time' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

if ($svc -and $svc.Status -eq 'Running' -and $svc.StartType -eq 'Automatic') {
    Write-Output 'W32Time healthy: running and automatic'
    exit 0
}
else {
    Write-Output 'W32Time not running or not automatic'
    exit 1
}
```

The **last line on stdout** becomes the *pre-remediation output* in reporting, so make it human-readable.

## Writing the remediation script

Remediation must be **idempotent** — running it on an already-fixed device must be harmless and produce the same end state. Always wrap changes in `try/catch` and exit non-zero on failure so Intune records the failure.

```powershell
try {
    Set-Service -Name 'W32Time' -StartupType Automatic -ErrorAction Stop
    Start-Service -Name 'W32Time' -ErrorAction Stop
    Write-Output 'W32Time set to Automatic and started'
    exit 0
}
catch {
    Write-Output "Remediation failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    exit 1
}
```

Because this runs on a schedule, re-running on a healthy device simply re-asserts the desired state with no harm.

## Context and bitness matter

Two settings change behaviour. **Run this script using the logged-on credentials** controls whether the script runs as the user (needed for `HKCU` and per-user settings) or as **SYSTEM** (the default, for machine-wide changes). **Run script in 64-bit PowerShell** should be **Yes** whenever you touch 64-bit registry hives or program paths — otherwise the script runs 32-bit and gets redirected to `WOW6432Node`, hiding the real state.

## Deploying and reading results

You assign a remediation to a **device or user group** with a schedule (once, hourly, or daily). Intune then shows, per device, the detection status and remediation status. You can also manage remediations through Graph as `deviceHealthScript` resources.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All'

# List your remediation (device health) scripts via Graph
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/deviceHealthScripts' |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty value |
    Select-Object displayName, id
```

Start with **detection only** (a remediation that just reports) to size the problem, then add the fix and pilot it on a small ring.

## Your task

Build a complete remediation pair for a real issue: a stale DNS cache or a disabled firewall profile (your choice). The **detection** script must read-only check the condition, write a clear single-line status, and exit 0 or 1 correctly. The **remediation** script must fix it **idempotently**, wrap changes in `try/catch`, and exit 0 on success and 1 on failure. State which context (SYSTEM or user) and bitness it needs and why. Finally, use `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` to list the `deviceHealthScripts` in your tenant.

slides.title: Intune proactive remediations
slides.sub: Month 2 - Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale  |  Lesson 4
slides.narration: This is one of the most powerful tools in modern endpoint engineering: self-healing devices. Intune proactive remediations let you ship a pair of scripts, one that finds a problem and one that fixes it, to thousands of machines on a schedule. By the end you will write a correct detection and remediation pair and understand the exit-code contract that ties them together.

slides.title: The detection plus remediation model
bullets: Two scripts run via the Intune Management Extension.
Detection decides if a problem exists.
Remediation fixes it when detection says so.
They talk through an exit-code contract.
slides.narration: A proactive remediation, now just called a remediation in Intune, is a pair of PowerShell scripts that run on a schedule through the Intune Management Extension. The first is a detection script that decides whether a problem exists. The second is a remediation script that fixes it. The two communicate through a strict exit code contract, and getting that contract right is the whole game. Crucially, the pair model lets you measure how widespread an issue is before you change a single device.

slides.title: The exit-code contract
bullets: Detection exit 0 means healthy, do nothing.
Detection exit 1 means problem found, remediate.
Any other behaviour is a script error.
Use exit, and mind $LASTEXITCODE.
slides.code:
if ($healthy) { Write-Output 'OK'; exit 0 }
else          { Write-Output 'Needs fix'; exit 1 }
slides.narration: Here is the contract, and it is simple but unforgiving. From the detection script, exit code zero means the device is healthy, so do nothing. Exit code one means a problem was found, so run the remediation. That is it. Get this backwards and you either never remediate or you remediate healthy machines. Use the exit keyword explicitly with the right number, and be aware of the dollar last exit code automatic variable when you call other tools.

slides.title: Writing detection
bullets: Fast, read-only, decisive.
Output one clear status line to stdout.
That last line shows up in Intune reports.
Then exit 0 or 1.
slides.narration: A good detection script is fast, read only, and decisive. It checks a condition, writes a short human readable status line with Write dash Output, then exits with the right code. That status matters because the last line you write to standard output becomes the pre remediation output shown in the Intune report. Here we check whether the Windows Time service is running and set to automatic. If yes, exit zero. If not, write why and exit one.

slides.title: Writing remediation
bullets: Must be idempotent: safe to re-run.
Wrap changes in try/catch.
Exit 0 on success, non-zero on failure.
Re-running just re-asserts the desired state.
slides.narration: The remediation script must be idempotent. That word means running it again on an already fixed device must be harmless and produce the same end state. Because remediations run on a schedule, this is non negotiable. Always wrap your changes in try catch, exit zero when the fix succeeds, and exit non zero when it fails so Intune records the failure honestly. Here we set the service to automatic and start it. Run it twice and nothing bad happens, it just re asserts the state.

slides.title: Context: SYSTEM vs user
bullets: Default context is SYSTEM, for machine-wide changes.
Run as logged-on user for HKCU and per-user settings.
Pick the context the change actually requires.
Wrong context is a common cause of 'fixed but not'.
slides.code:
# HKLM and services -> SYSTEM context
# HKCU and per-user settings -> user context
slides.narration: Two settings change how your scripts behave, and the first is context. By default a remediation runs as the local SYSTEM account, which is right for machine wide changes like services and the H K L M hive. But if you need to touch a per user setting or the H K C U hive, you must choose to run it in the logged on user context. Picking the wrong context is a classic cause of a remediation that reports success but does not actually fix what the user sees. Match the context to the change.

slides.title: Bitness: run 64-bit
bullets: Scripts can run 32-bit by default.
32-bit gets redirected to WOW6432Node.
Set 'Run in 64-bit PowerShell' to Yes for 64-bit state.
Otherwise you may read the wrong registry view.
slides.code:
# Set 'Run script in 64-bit PowerShell' = Yes
# when reading 64-bit registry or program paths
slides.narration: The second setting is bitness. By default your script can run in thirty two bit PowerShell, and on modern Windows that means registry and file system calls get quietly redirected to the W O W six four three two Node view. So if you read a sixty four bit registry key or a sixty four bit program path, set Run script in sixty four bit PowerShell to Yes. Otherwise your detection reads the wrong view, sees the wrong state, and your whole remediation gives wrong answers. When in doubt, run sixty four bit.

slides.title: Deploy and read results via Graph
bullets: Assign to a device or user group with a schedule.
Intune reports detection and remediation status per device.
Manage scripts as deviceHealthScript in Graph.
Pilot detection-only first to size the problem.
slides.code:
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
  -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/deviceHealthScripts' |
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty value |
  Select-Object displayName, id
slides.narration: You assign a remediation to a device or user group with a schedule, once, hourly, or daily, and Intune then reports detection and remediation status for every device. You can also manage these through Graph, where they appear as device health script resources. A pro move: deploy detection only first, a remediation that just reports and never changes anything, to size how widespread the issue really is. Then add the fix and pilot it on a small ring before going wide.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Detection exits 0 healthy, 1 needs fix.
Remediation must be idempotent with try/catch.
Match context and bitness to the change.
Pilot detection-only, then ring out the fix.
Task: build a full remediation pair plus a Graph list.
slides.narration: Let us recap. Detection exits zero for healthy and one when a fix is needed. The remediation must be idempotent, wrapped in try catch, exiting zero on success and non zero on failure. Match the context, SYSTEM or user, and the bitness to the change you are making. And pilot detection only first, then ring out the fix. Your task: build a complete remediation pair for a stale D N S cache or a disabled firewall profile. Detection read only, one clear status line, correct exit code. Remediation idempotent, try catch, exit zero or one. State the context and bitness it needs and why. Then use Invoke dash M g Graph Request to list the device health scripts in your tenant. See you in lesson five.
